scenes.text: About a hundred years ago, many astronomers thought our Milky Way was the entire universe.
Those fuzzy spirals in the night sky were thought to be clouds inside it.
In nineteen twenty, Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis argued about it in a famous Great Debate.
Then Edwin Hubble used the biggest telescope in the world.
It was the hundred inch Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson, in California.
In October nineteen twenty three, he spotted a star in Andromeda that kept getting brighter and dimmer.
He marked it on the photo in red: VAR, with an exclamation mark.
It was a Cepheid, a kind of star that Henrietta Leavitt had shown can measure distance.
Slower pulsing Cepheids are brighter, so its rhythm revealed how far away it was.
Hubble's answer was about nine hundred thousand light years, far outside the Milky Way.
Today we know Andromeda is even farther, about two and a half million light years away.
The news first appeared on November twenty third, nineteen twenty four, in a tiny New York Times story.
Now, astronomers estimate the universe holds up to several trillion galaxies.
How does it feel to be one tiny speck in all of that?

title: The day we learned other galaxies exist 🌌
caption: On Nov 23, 1924, the New York Times reported that Edwin Hubble had found Andromeda is a separate galaxy, thanks to a Cepheid star he spotted with the 100-inch Hooker telescope. Before that, many thought the Milky Way was the whole universe.
